query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The phase stability of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between a composition‐dependent free-energy penalty for retaining its high-temperature BCC state and the kinetic barriers for nucleation. When the annealing temperature/time is increased past a critical point (as predicted by CALPHAD free-energy calculations), the free-energy penalty exceeds the reduced nucleation barrier (mediated by interfacial energies and short-range order changes), triggering the nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature metastable BCC state
generation.intervention: A systematic annealing study that varies temperature and holding time near the CALPHAD-predicted instability threshold at this fixed composition
generation.conditions: Controlled annealing experiments with fixed composition, where samples are heated to temperatures near the predicted free-energy instability point and held for varying times to allow kinetics to overcome nucleation barriers
generation.structural_mediator: Local nucleation sites influenced by interfacial energies and short-range ordering which mediate the transformation from the BCC phase to secondary phases
generation.mechanism: At higher annealing temperatures or longer holding times, the thermodynamic free-energy penalty for sustaining the BCC phase increases and eventually overcomes the kinetic nucleation barrier. This results in the onset of precipitate formation and phase separation, as the system transforms to lower its overall free energy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Above a critical combination of temperature and hold time, microstructural analysis should reveal the initiation and growth of secondary phases (e.g., a precipitate phase) from the initial single BCC matrix, with the fraction of secondary phases increasing with further annealing.
generation.baseline: Annealing at lower temperatures or with insufficient hold time will maintain the single-phase BCC structure, as the kinetic barriers are not overcome despite a moderate thermodynamic instability.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to occur only in the temperature and time regime near the computed free-energy instability threshold; outside this range (i.e., at significantly lower temperatures or very short annealing times), the BCC phase will remain metastable.
generation.uncertainty: Exact critical values for temperature and hold time are not precisely known and may be influenced by sample inhomogeneity and experimental variability. Additionally, the quantitative interplay between thermodynamic driving force and nucleation kinetics has inherent uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples, and conduct annealing treatments at incremental temperatures and hold times bracketing the CALPHAD-derived instability threshold. Characterize the microstructure post-annealing using TEM, SEM, and XRD to detect the onset and progression of secondary phase formation. Compare samples annealed just below and above the predicted threshold.
measurements: Phase identification and volume fraction via XRD and TEM
Observation and quantification of precipitate nucleation and growth using SEM/TEM
Measurement of short-range order or interfacial energies if feasible
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples annealed above the predicted temperature/time threshold do not exhibit any detectable secondary phase formation or a measurable change in microstructure compared to the baseline single-phase BCC state, then the hypothesis that a thermodynamic instability overcoming a kinetic barrier governs the phase transition is falsified.

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [7] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ] This well‐established mechanism highlights the central role of brittle phase precipitation and element segregation at GBs in governing embrittlement in conventional alloys.

In contrast, emerging high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), [ [15] , [16] , [17] ] which consist of multiple principal elements, introduce new thermodynamic and kinetic complexities that challenge conventional thermal exposure paradigms. Their high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion kinetics [ [

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys have shown that modifying Al content and thermal histories (via variations in processing, irradiation, and aging treatments) leads to dramatic changes in phase constitution. Initial work (e.g., PMC4999872) demonstrated that low-Al alloys maintained a single-phase structure while higher-Al variants underwent nano-scale precipitation and phase separation under external stimuli, indicating a thermodynamic drive toward instability when Al increases. More recent studies (e.g., PMC12806431) on eutectic AlCoCrFeNi alloys revealed that even small changes in thermal treatment can trigger transitions (such as tempering-like embrittlement) linked with distinct phase boundary phenomena, yet none of these efforts have unified the competing thermodynamic signals with the kinetic barriers that delay or enable these transformations.
decision.unsolved: What remains unsolved is a single, testable mechanism that quantitatively predicts phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 by linking a composition-dependent thermodynamic instability (a free-energy driving force for phase separation/decomposition) with the kinetic thresholds for nucleation (governed by interfacial energies and short-range ordering). The challenge is to define baseline conditions and controlled comparisons that can isolate these concurrent effects and articulate a clearly falsifiable prediction.
decision.lever: A systematic annealing study that varies temperature and holding time near the thermodynamically predicted instability threshold (as computed via CALPHAD) at a fixed composition (Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7). The key lever is controlling the annealing time/temperature to probe when the BCC phase transitions to secondary phases owing to reduced nucleation barriers.
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the gap by decoupling the thermodynamic driving force from kinetic hindrances. It tests the hypothesis that once the free-energy penalty for maintaining the high-temperature BCC phase exceeds a critical value and the corresponding kinetic barriers (e.g., interfacial energy and nucleation activation energy) are overcome, a measurable transformation (e.g., onset of precipitate formation) will occur. A failure to observe such a transition under these controlled conditions would falsify the proposed mechanistic link between composition-dependent thermodynamic instability and kinetic nucleation thresholds.
